General Epistles
JEN-uh-rul ih-PIS-ulz
noun phrase (biblical category)
From Old French general (universal, from Latin generalis, of a kind or class, from genus, kind, race) + Latin epistola (a letter, from Greek epistolē, a message or letter, from epi- + stellō, to send, equip). Also called the “Catholic Epistles,” from Greek katholikos (universal, from kata- through + holos whole). The letters are “general” or “catholic” because most are addressed not to a specific local congregation or individual but to the church broadly scattered throughout the Roman world.

Biblical Definition

The General Epistles (also called the Catholic Epistles) are the seven New Testament letters not attributed to Paul: the Epistle of James, First and Second Peter, First, Second, and Third John, and the Epistle of Jude. They are addressed to broad or universal audiences — “the twelve tribes scattered abroad” (Jas. 1:1), “strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Pet. 1:1), “those who are called, sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ” (Jude 1:1) — rather than to a named local church. Despite their variety of authorship, setting, and emphasis, these letters share a common pastoral urgency: they address communities under threat from false teaching, persecution, and moral drift, calling the elect to perseverance, holiness, and doctrinal fidelity. First Peter is the supreme epistle of elect exiles under suffering; James is the epistle of a living faith proved in deeds; First John is the epistle of assurance and fellowship in the light; Jude is the concentrated polemic of contending for the once-delivered faith. Second Peter confronts false teachers with the certainty of divine judgment; Second and Third John are brief pastoral dispatches on truth and hospitality. Together the General Epistles form a comprehensive pastoral theology of the church under pressure — the apostles’ pastoral counsel to scattered congregations facing the same temptations every generation of the church has faced.

Webster 1828 Definition

The seven New Testament letters not attributed to Paul — James, 1–2 Peter, 1–3 John, and Jude — addressed to broad rather than congregation-specific audiences and forming together a comprehensive pastoral theology of the church under trial, persecution, and false teaching.

GENERAL EPISTLES, n. pl. [also: Catholic Epistles, Universal Epistles] The seven New Testament letters not attributed to Paul: James; First Peter; Second Peter; First John; Second John; Third John; Jude. Some traditions extend the term to include Hebrews where Pauline authorship is questioned.

2. The term “catholic” (general, universal) reflects that these letters address believers broadly — the scattered diaspora, the elect throughout the Roman provinces — rather than a single named congregation. It does not imply Roman Catholic authorship or reception.

3. Canonical recognition: Eusebius (ca. A.D. 313) listed several as “disputed” (antilegomena) not because their content was doubted by orthodox churches but because some circulated less widely than others. By the councils of Laodicea (363) and Carthage (397) all seven were universally recognized.

4. Unifying themes: the elect exile living as a stranger in a hostile world (1 Pet.); the faith that proves itself in deeds of mercy and impartial love (Jas.); the antichrist spirit already at work against orthodox Christology (1 John; 2 John); the false teachers who crept in unawares (Jude; 2 Pet.); the faithful elder and the gospel community (3 John).

Key Scripture

Jude 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

James 1:22 — "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

1 Peter 1:3 — "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,"

1 John 1:9 — "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

Modern Corruption

Historical-critical scholarship’s denial of apostolic authorship for several of the General Epistles — treating 2 Peter and Jude as pseudonymous, 1 John as a school product — undermines the canonical authority these letters rest on, effectively demoting them from apostolic word to post-apostolic devout fiction.

expand to see more

Modern historical-critical scholarship has treated several General Epistles as pseudonymous — written by later authors in the names of James, Peter, or Jude but not actually composed by them. The arguments rest on stylistic analysis, assumed theological development, and claims about Greek literacy levels among Galilean fishermen. These are methodological preferences, not demonstrated facts. The Reformed confessional tradition holds that all seven letters bear genuine apostolic or near-apostolic authorship: James the Lord’s brother; Peter the apostle; John the apostle and beloved disciple; Jude the Lord’s brother. The claim that Peter could not have written 2 Peter in polished Greek ignores that 1 Peter itself acknowledges Silvanus (Silas) as a scribe (1 Pet. 5:12) — the use of an amanuensis was standard practice in antiquity and is not evidence of later pseudonymous composition.

Within progressive Christianity, the General Epistles are selectively quarried for comfortable passages — 1 John’s “God is love,” James’s concern for the poor — while the harder passages are explained away as culturally limited. Second Peter 2’s fierce denunciation of false teachers and Jude’s sustained polemic are treated as uncharitable and sub-Christian in spirit. This reading misunderstands the apostolic pattern: the same John who wrote “God is love” (1 John 4:8) also wrote “if anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house” (2 John 10). Love for the flock and war against wolves are not opposites in the General Epistles; they are partners, two sides of the same pastoral faithfulness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin generalis (universal, for all classes) + epistola (letter); the “general” designation identifies these letters by their broad, non-congregation-specific address — unlike Paul’s church-specific correspondence, the General Epistles speak to the scattered church as a whole.

expand to see more

Greek katholikos — universal, general, from kata- (down through, according to) + holos (whole); the Catholic Epistles are so named because they address the whole church, not because they belong to the Roman Catholic tradition

Greek epistolē — a letter, from epi- (upon) + stellō (to send, equip); the apostolic letters were dispatched to equip the churches for the tasks of their calling — they are pastoral dispatches, not academic treatises

Latin diaspora — a scattering (from Greek dia- through + speirein to sow); James and 1 Peter address the elect diaspora — God’s people scattered as strangers in the world, an ecclesiological category that includes every believing congregation

Greek antilegomena — the disputed ones (from anti- against + legein to speak); Eusebius’s early-fourth-century classification of these letters reflected varying circulation, not doubt about their apostolic content or theological authority

Greek hapax — once for all; Jude’s “once for all delivered” (v. 3) stands as the General Epistles’ collective motto — these letters are the apostolic charge to guard, not to revise, the faith they received

Usage

"The category “General Epistles” is a practical organizing tool for preaching: these seven letters together offer a complete pastoral theology of perseverance, discernment, and holiness for churches under pressure — they are the apostles’ last words to a scattered flock facing false teaching and imperial hostility."

"Jude occupies a unique place among the General Epistles as the shortest and most concentrated polemic — essentially a compressed warning that presupposes 2 Peter’s argument about false teachers and assumes the reader’s prior knowledge of Old Testament judicial history (the Exodus generation, the fallen angels, Sodom and Gomorrah)."

"First John and the two brief Johannine letters form a distinctive cluster — sharing vocabulary (light, love, truth, fellowship), a consistent theology of assurance and Christological confession, and a sharp line between the spirit of truth and the spirit of antichrist — the apostolic hand that wrote the Fourth Gospel also wrote these three."
